pillar_reactions.evidence: Volunteered a positive reaction and articulated the value proposition back in his own words: 'I like the fact how this is dynamic movements and I think one of them, Trevor, said they were, instead of being robotic in a gym, which I got to thinking, said, yeah, that is all robotic... So the kettlebells did seem to have, the way Trevor does, definitely has some fluidity to it.' He was already doing Trevor's five-minute mobility routine most mornings and confirmed the daily commitment would be no problem: 'that would be no problem doing the flexibility.'

Driven mostly by his wife, who asked the substantive question — 'what's your normal, you know, Trevor says, clean up your eating, what, is it just like cut out sugar, everything we already know, pretty much, or does he have a specific meal plan?' — and attached a clinical caution the rep did not address: 'he does have high cholesterol, the LDL, so I want to be cautious of that.' The prospect engaged honestly and self-diagnosed his own gap as quantity rather than quality: 'I think my problem is, I think you hit on it, it's quantity. I tend to overeat.' The couple also held each other to account on the daily peanut butter, which the rep noted approvingly.

Agreed and tied the teach-you-to-leave framing directly to what he wanted: 'that's what I'd like it's just I don't need to be in it for the rest of my life just teach me what I need to know and then I'll move on by myself.' He then asked a run of practical questions about the Thursday live workout — its time, whether it is genuinely live, whether it separates beginner from advanced, and whether it clashes with their yoga — which is engaged rather than resistant. He also probed the flexibility of the programme: 'So he'll switch it up instead of saying, no, you got to stick with it?'

anchors.raw: I was thinking around two, two or between two and three, but okay, so it's twice as much as I thought.
anchors.note: A concrete internal anchor at $2,000-3,000 against a $6,000 offer, which the rep himself reported to the setter thirteen minutes later as 'they had sort of a price shock, and it's like, ooh, it's twice as much as they expected.' The source of the figure was never established and is worth establishing, given that a $199 per month product is publicly advertised and produced a comparable anchor on the 07/02 call.

anchors.raw: I could put it like this, I could continue to watch YouTube videos for a lot cheaper. Because I do follow him on a day, Trevor, on a daily basis. And he always puts his workouts in the captions, you know.
anchors.competitor: Trevor's own free YouTube content, including published workouts in the captions
anchors.note: The competing product is the company's own free marketing, and the prospect is already using it — he had done Trevor's weighted squat video and does the five-minute mobility routine most mornings. The rep conceded it works ('if you follow the YouTube, you can see results, 100%. Otherwise, you wouldn't post it'), which is honest but leaves the paid offer defended only by customisation and form correction. The prospect argued himself back across the gap unprompted: 'But not the same. I know it's not the same. This is a lot more in-depth.'

anchors.raw: I think about gym memberships. think about what another back surgery would cost. You know, that's probably a lot too cheap.
anchors.competitor: The cost of a second back surgery in the United States
anchors.note: The one genuinely supportive anchor in the batch, and the prospect supplied it himself before hearing the price — he reasoned that whatever the figure is, it is cheap against another spinal operation. The rep picked it up and built the value case on it: 'if you want to make sure you actually get the results that you want and you don't have to get surgery again, then I think in the long run, this is going to cost less.' Effective commercially, and the reason it is also recorded as a compliance flag.

unmet_demand.want: Confidence that loaded kettlebell training is safe for a surgically repaired spine, in a man who says outright that he fears loading it
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Never established. The rep asked whether a specialist had been seen, was told no, and moved on without suggesting one or seeking clearance. The prospect's most recent imaging is three years old, his working diagnosis came from ChatGPT, and the assurance he received was 'we're not clinical people... We have seen it work with so many people. So we know it works.'

unmet_demand.want: Nutrition guidance that accounts for high LDL cholesterol, raised explicitly by his wife as something to be cautious about
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Not addressed at any point. The rep acknowledged the comment and went straight into the standard three-part nutrition framework — eating windows, intermittent fasting, whole foods — without referencing cholesterol, and it was never returned to.

unmet_demand.want: Recourse if the programme does not reduce his back pain — 'if it's not for me, I don't have any recourse'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Met, but only by improvisation. No refund policy, trial or cancellation right exists in the offer; the rep created a 30-day exit on the call to answer it. The guarantee that does exist runs the other way, extending coaching rather than returning money, and does not address a buyer who wants out.

unmet_demand.want: Clarity on whether two people in a household can train on one purchase, and at what price
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Raised near the end of the call and left unanswered. The claim that it would 'cut the price in half if two people are doing it' was not confirmed or corrected, and the rep responded only that he has 'seen many people do it with their family'. The couple leave with an unresolved and possibly false price expectation going into a joint decision.
